messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 6 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'Dual-Boost-Rect': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (Single-Sync-Boost); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

[c0034] P-SSHI  (topology 40eae91a637a, score 4.83, conditions passed 0/6)
D1 D pzp out DSCH
D2 D pzn out DSCH
D3 D 0 pzp DSCH
D4 D 0 pzn DSCH
L1 L pzp n1 0.000917
S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
G1 SYNC ton=1.23e-05s phase=0.17 edges=both
C1 C out 0 4.7e-05
DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1    -0.0296 -0.0256    7.92       -  8.84e-05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2    -0.0293 -0.0253    7.92       -  0.000127  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3      0.199   0.216    33.7       -    0.0018  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S4    -0.0578 -0.0553     4.8       -  0.000152  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok

failing: S4 vout_min: -0.05775 V (needs >= 1.8 V, margin -1.03)
S5 vout_min: -0.03799 V (needs >= 1.8 V, margin -1.02)

S1 startup: not reached / not measured (needs <= 0.4 s, margin -1.00)

... and 5 more failing checks
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: 11.3 uW of 0.476 uW needed (2364 %); S4: 6.69 uW of 0.147 uW needed (4542 %); S6: 7.72 uW of 0.324 uW needed (2383 %)
value sizing: 48/48 evaluations (finished: budget used)
what this means:
- V(out) never exceeds 0.22 V on any condition: no charge reaches the storage, or something conducts from out to ground (check every diode's orientation: nodes are [anode, cathode])

Topologies explored so far (hash: name, best score):
  40eae91a637a: P-SSHI (4.83)

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{out\_min} \ge 1.8$ V
        *   $v_{out\_max} \le 3.6$ V
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05$ V
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s
        *   $dv \le 0.02$ V
    *   Piezo properties: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p = 25$ nF and $R_{leak} = 20$ M$\Omega$.
    *   Open circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V. This is very low compared to the required $1.8$ V output.
    *   Crucial: Since $V_{oc} < 1.8$ V, a simple rectifier (FBR) will not work (as shown in the reference design). We need a DC-DC boost-like mechanism.

    *   P-SSHI (Parallel-SSHI) failed miserably. The $v_{out}$ barely moved (around 0.2 V).
    *   Looking at P-SSHI components:
        *   $D_1$: pzp $\to$ out
        *   $D_2$: pzn $\to$ out
        *   $D_3$: 0 $\to$ pzp
        *   $D_4$: 0 $\to$ pzn
        *   $L_1$: pzp $\to$ n1
        *   $S_1$: n1 $\to$ pzn
        *   $G_1$: SYNC
        *   $C_1$: out $\to$ 0
        *   $DZ_1$: 0 $\to$ out (Zener)
    *   Wait, if $V_{out}$ is 1.8 V and $D_1$ is pzp $\to$ out, $D_1$ is reverse-biased unless $V_{pzp} > 1.8 + 0.25 = 2.05$ V. But $V_{oc}$ is only 0.76 V. The only way to get $V_{pzp} > 2$ V is through the inductor $L_1$ kicking back.
    *   In P-SSHI, the inductor $L_1$ is in series with the piezo. $S_1$ shorts the inductor across the piezo. This is a standard SSHI-like approach.
    *   However, the current results show $v_{out}$ stayed near 0V. This suggests that either the energy isn't being transferred or it's being clamped.
    *   Wait, the "screen" test (out fixed at 1.8 V) showed $S_2: 11.3 \mu$W, $S_4: 6.69 \mu$W, $S_6: 7.72 \mu$W. These are actually *higher* than the load needs. This means the topology *can* deliver power, but the closed-loop simulation (starting from 0V) fails. Why?
    *   Maybe the startup is the problem? Or the diode configuration?

    *   $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V.
    *   Requirement: $V_{out} \ge 1.8$ V.
    *   Since $V_{oc} < V_{out}$, we must use an inductive boost mechanism.
    *   A standard SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) usually flips the voltage across $C_p$ to maximize extraction.
    *   The most basic inductive boost for piezo is to charge an inductor and then dump it into a capacitor via a diode.

    *   The "screen" test succeeded, but the simulation didn't. This often means the circuit cannot start from 0V.
    *   In P-SSHI, the diodes $D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4$ form a full bridge.
    *   $D_1$ [pzp, out], $D_2$ [pzn, out], $D_3$ [0, pzp], $D_4$ [0, pzn].
    *   Current from piezo flows through $D_3$ or $D_4$ to ground, and through $D_1$ or $D_2$ to $V_{out}$.
    *   If $V_{out}$ starts at 0, the bridge should work like an FBR. The FBR reference design gave $v_{avg} \approx 0.56$ V.
    *   Why did P-SSHI fail to reach 0.56 V?
    *   Ah, look at the inductor: $L_1$ is between `pzp` and `n1`, and $S_1$ is between `n1` and `pzn`.
    *   When $S_1$ is open, the current from the piezo at node `pzp` must go through $L_1$. This is fine.
    *   When $S_1$ is closed, the inductor $L_1$ is connected between `pzp` and `pzn`. This is the "flip" phase.
    *   Wait, if the inductor is always in the path from `pzp` to the rectifier, and $L_1$ is small, it's just a resistor. But if $L_1$ is too large, does it block current? No, it's an inductor.
    *   Actually, let's look at the P-SSHI topology again: $L_1$ is between `pzp` and `n1`, and $S_1$ is between `n1` and `pzn`.
    *   This means $L_1$ is *only* in the path from `pzp` to `pzn` when $S_1$ is closed.
    *   When $S_1$ is open, the path from `pzp` to the bridge is still there.
    *   So why did it fail? Maybe the tuned $L_1$ value was too large, or the SYNC timing was wrong?
    *   Wait, the screen test (where $V_{out}$ is fixed) shows it *can* deliver power. The problem is "cold start".

    *   Let's try a simpler "Boost-Rect" (though the hash says it was explored). Let's think of a different one.
    *   Maybe a "Single-ended" approach?
    *   Piezo $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Diode $\to$ Out.
    *   Switch to ground to build up energy in the inductor.
    *   Wait, the piezo is a current source. To build energy in an inductor, we need to allow the current to flow into it.
    *   If we have: `pzp` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `n1`, and a switch `S1` from `n1` $\to$ `0`.
    *   When `S1` is closed, $L_1$ is charged by the piezo current.
    *   When `S1` is open, the energy in $L_1$ is pushed through a diode $D_1$ from `n1` $\to$ `out`.
    *   This is a classic boost converter. Since it's a piezo, the "input" is the $C_p$ capacitance.

    *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn` (with `pzn` grounded for simplicity, or using a bridge).
    *   If we ground `pzn`:
        *   `pzp` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `n1`
        *   `S1` from `n1` $\to$ `0`
        *   `D1` from `n1` $\to$ `out`
        *   `C1` from `out` $\to$ `0`
    *   Operation:
        1.  `S1` closes: $L_1$ is connected to ground. The piezo current $I_p$ charges $C_p$ and $L_1$.
        2.  `S1` opens: The current in $L_1$ must continue. It flows through $D_1$ to `out`.
    *   Wait, this only works if the piezo is a voltage source. With a current source, $I_p$ flows into $C_p$ and $L_1$.
    *   Let's refine:
        *   `pzp` and `pzn` are the terminals.
        *   Let's use a bridge to get a DC voltage across a capacitor $C_{in}$, then boost it.
        *   But we have a limit of 16 components.
        *   Bridge: 4 diodes. $C_{in}$: 1 cap. Boost: 1 L, 1 S, 1 D. Total: 7. This is feasible.
    *   However, the piezo $V_{oc}$ is very low (0.76 V). A bridge will give about 0.5 V. Boosting 0.5 V to 1.8 V is easy.

    *   Wait, can we do it without a bridge to save components?
    *   A "Half-bridge" boost:
        *   `pzp` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `n1`
        *   `D1` [n1, out]
        *   `S1` [n1, pzn]
        *   This is essentially the P-SSHI but without the other diodes.
        *   Let's try a more robust boost:
            1.  `pzp` $\to$ `D1` $\to$ `n_in`
            2.  `pzn` $\to$ `D2` $\to$ `n_in` (Wait, this is wrong. Need a bridge).
            3.  Bridge: `pzp` $\to$ `D1` $\to$ `out_pre`, `pzn` $\to$ `D2` $\to$ `out_pre`, `0` $\to$ `D3` $\to$ `pzp`, `0` $\to$ `D4` $\to$ `pzn`.
            4.  Now `out_pre` has a DC voltage.
            5.  Boost from `out_pre`: `out_pre` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `n1`, `S1` [n1, 0], `D5` [n1, out].
            6.  This uses 4+1+1+1+1 = 8 components.

    *   Wait, if $V_{oc}$ is only 0.76 V, the bridge output $V_{pre}$ will be around 0.5 V. The boost converter needs a switch $S_1$ to drive $L_1$. The SYNC controller can do this.
    *   The SYNC controller closes the switch at the piezo voltage extrema.
    *   Let's try a "Synchronous Boost" that works directly with the piezo:
        *   `L1` from `pzp` to `n1`.
        *   `S1` from `n1` to `pzn`.
        *   `D1` from `n1` to `out`.
        *   `C1` from `out` to `0`.
        *   `D2` from `pzn` to `0` (to ground `pzn` via a diode).
        *   This is a bit like the "Single-Sync-Boost" which was already explored.

    *   The "P-SSHI" had `D1, D2, D3, D4` (bridge) and `L1, S1`.
    *   Wait, the P-SSHI I saw in the results:
        `D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]`
        `L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn]`
    *   In this config, $L_1$ is in *series* with the bridge for the `pzp` side.
    *   If `S1` is open, current from `pzp` goes through $L_1$ to `D1` or `D3`.
    *   If `S1` is closed, $L_1$ is shorted across the piezo (`pzp` to `pzn`).
    *   This is an SSHI circuit. The goal of SSHI is to flip the voltage on $C_p$ to avoid the $V_{oc}$ limit.
    *   The reason it might have failed is that $V_{out}$ is too high for the flipped voltage to reach it.
    *   Wait, if $V_{out} = 1.8$ V and $V_{oc} = 0.76$ V, the peak voltage after flipping is $2 \cdot V_{oc} \approx 1.52$ V. Still not enough to pass through a diode (1.52 - 0.25 = 1.27 V) into a 1.8 V capacitor.
    *   *Self-correction:* SSHI can't boost the voltage *above* the flipped peak unless there is another boost stage.

    *   Since we need to get from $\sim 0.7$ V to $1.8$ V, and the flipped voltage $2 V_{oc}$ is only $\sim 1.5$ V, we MUST have a boost converter (an inductor that stores energy and then releases it at a higher voltage).
    *   The most reliable boost converter:
        1.  Charge inductor $L$ with a constant current (or from a source).
        2.  Flyback the energy into the output capacitor.

    *   Let's try this:
        -   Rectify the piezo first to get a small DC voltage $V_{pre}$ on $C_{pre}$.
        -   Use a boost converter to step $V_{pre}$ up to $V_{out}$.
        -   But we only have 2 SYNCs. We can use one SYNC to operate the boost switch.

    *   *Alternative:* A "Charge Pump" (but we have inductors, which are better).

    *   *Let's try a "Boost-Rect" again, but carefully:*
        -   `pzp` $\to$ `D1` $\to$ `n_pre`
        -   `pzn` $\to$ `D2` $\to$ `n_pre`
        -   `0` $\to$ `D3` $\to$ `pzp`
        -   `0` $\to$ `D4` $\to$ `pzn`
        -   `C_pre` from `n_pre` $\to$ `0`
        -   `n_pre` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `n_boost`
        -   `S1` from `n_boost` $\to$ `0`
        -   `D5` from `n_boost` $\to$ `out`
        -   `C_out` from `out` $\to$ `0`
        -   `DZ1` from `0` $\to$ `out` (zener clamp)

    *   *Wait, the SYNC controller:* It triggers at the piezo's voltage extrema.
    *   In the circuit above, the boost switch `S1` would need to switch at a frequency independent of the piezo (e.g., 10 kHz). But our SYNC controller is tied to the piezo frequency (100 Hz).
    *   If we switch `S1` at 100 Hz, the boost converter might be too slow.
    *   Let's check: $f = 100$ Hz, $T = 10$ ms. $t_{on} = 1$ ms (max).
    *   With $L = 1$ mH, $\Delta I = (V/L) \cdot t_{on} = (0.5/1\text{e-3}) \cdot 1\text{e-3} = 0.5$ A.
    *   Energy $E = 0.5 \cdot L \cdot I^2 = 0.5 \cdot 1\text{e-3} \cdot 0.5^2 = 125 \mu$J.
    *   Is this enough? $P_{load} \approx 1.8^2 / 10\text{M}\Omega = 0.324 \mu$W.
    *   Energy per cycle needed: $0.324 \mu\text{W} \cdot 0.01\text{s} = 3.24$ nJ.
    *   Yes, 100 Hz is plenty of speed.

    -   S1: `pzp` $\to$ `D1` $\to$ `n_pre`
    -   S2: `pzn` $\to$ `D2` $\to$ `n_pre`
    -   S3: `0` $\to$ `D3` $\to$ `pzp`
    -   S4: `0` $\to$ `D4` $\to$ `pzn`
    -   `C_pre`: `n_pre` $\to$ `0`
    -   `L1`: `n_pre` $\to$ `n_boost`
    -   `S1`: `n_boost` $\to$ `0`
    -   `D5`: `n_boost` $\to$ `out`
    -   `C_out`: `out` $\to$ `0`
    -   `DZ1`: `0` $\to$ `out`
    -   `G1`: SYNC (controls `S1`)

    *   Wait, if the SYNC is tied to the piezo, $S_1$ will close at the peaks.
    *   When $S_1$ is closed, $L_1$ is connected to ground, so it charges from `n_pre`.
    *   When $S_1$ opens, $L_1$ dumps into `out`.
    *   This should work. Let's check component count:
        -   Diodes: D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, DZ1 (6)
        -   Capacitors: C_pre, C_out (2)
        -   Inductor: L1 (1)
        -   Switch: S1 (1)
        -   SYNC: G1 (1)
        -   Total: 11 components. Well within the 16-component limit.

    *   The "screen" test showed that $V_{out}$ fixed at 1.8 V allows power to flow.
    *   The "cold start" problem in P-SSHI was likely that $2 V_{oc}$ was not enough to push through the diode.
    *   In this Boost-Rect design:
        -   Initially, $V_{out} = 0$.
        -   The bridge will charge $C_{pre}$ to $\approx 0.5$ V.
        -   As soon as $C_{pre}$ has some voltage, the boost converter can start.
        -   $S_1$ closes, $L_1$ charges to $0.5$ V.
        -   $S_1$ opens, $L_1$ boosts the voltage to $V_{out}$.
        -   Since $V_{out}$ starts at 0, the boost can easily push $V_{out}$ up to 1.8 V.
        -   Once $V_{out}$ is 1.8 V, the boost converter continues to maintain it.

    *   `C_pre`: Needs to be large enough to keep $V_{pre}$ stable during the $L_1$ charging phase. Try $1 \mu$F.
    *   `L1`: Try $1$ mH.
    *   `C_out`: Try $2.2 \mu$F.
    *   `G1` (SYNC):
        -   `ton`: Try $1$ ms (max) to get maximum energy per cycle.
        -   `edges`: "both" to pump twice per period.
        -   `phase`: $0.0$.

    *   Let's refine the bridge:
